strengths: Addresses a genuine and important problem in MHQA dataset creation—automatic synthesis without expensive human annotation
Novel framework design: first to synthesize authentic multi-hop questions from raw corpora without human-provided documents, templates, or structured data
Well-formalized problem with clear mathematical constraints (Fact Distribution, No-Shortcut, Distributed Source) ensuring authentic multi-hop reasoning
Innovative two-stage retrieval mechanism with fine-tuned reranker using simulated feedback, showing strong ablation results
Comprehensive three-dimensional evaluation system (LLM-as-judge, answerability/difficulty, evidence-accessibility) with principled methodology
Strong empirical results: 96-99% multi-hop rate rivaling human datasets, consistent across multiple generator LLMs of varying scales
Detailed system design and reproducibility: extensive appendices, promised code release, multiple models evaluated, deterministic generation parameters
Well-engineered pipeline from bridge entity identification through retrieval to polishing with clear quality assurance steps
weaknesses: Critical methodological gap: no human evaluation to validate LLM-as-judge assessments; while the self-consistency argument is reasonable, completely avoiding human validation weakens claims about quality matching human datasets

Missing direct comparison against other automatic synthesis methods mentioned in related work (Lupidi et al., Luo et al., Wu et al.); only compared to human-annotated baselines, not synthesis approaches
Evaluation scale limited to 100 samples for quality assessment with no confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance estimates
Scope restricted to two question types (bridge, comparison); MHQA encompasses more diverse reasoning patterns, limiting generalizability
Only evaluated on English Wikipedia 2018; claims about value in specialized domains lack empirical support; no multi-domain or multi-corpus evaluation

Practical usability concerns: Support F1 scores are very low (0.17-0.22), meaning retrieving complete evidence sets is difficult despite individual document recall ~0.70; unclear how useful such hard questions are for actual MHQA systems
Heavy LLM dependency with significant performance variance across generators (89.8-98.9% multi-hop rate); acknowledged reproducibility issues with proprietary models; long-term viability uncertain
Insufficient failure analysis: no breakdown of failure modes, rejection rates not clearly reported, no analysis of which question types or document combinations fail
Hyperparameter choices lack thorough justification: MMR parameters from 'preliminary experiments', entity filtering threshold tied to single model, limited ablations on design decisions
Constraint validation incomplete: while constraints are formally defined, evidence of strict enforcement and violation rates not clearly reported

strengths: Addresses genuine practical problem: Creating MHQA datasets is expensive and time-consuming; this fully automatic approach requires no manual intervention, templates, or structured data
Well-formalized framework with explicit constraints (Fact Distribution, No-Shortcut, Distributed Source) that ensure authentic multi-hop reasoning
Innovative fine-tuning strategy using simulated feedback from the synthesis pipeline itself, reducing manual supervision needs

Comprehensive three-dimensional evaluation system (LLM-as-judge, answerability/difficulty, evidence-accessibility) with well-reasoned justification for prioritizing LLM self-consistency over human alignment
Strong empirical results: Synthesized questions achieve 96.4-98.9% multi-hop validity and 4.27-4.45 quality scores, meeting or exceeding human-annotated benchmarks across multiple dimensions
Rigorous reproducibility practices: Multiple open-source LLM options, detailed experimental settings, prompts in appendices, avoided self-enhancement bias, committed to code release
Convincing ablation studies demonstrating contributions of fine-tuned reranker (success rate 70.1%→75.3%) and polisher module
Two-stage coarse-to-fine retrieval with MMR and learned reranking is well-motivated and practically effective
weaknesses: Severely limited scope: Only addresses 2 of many MHQA patterns (bridge, comparison). Intersection, commonsense, and other reasoning types excluded. Claim of being 'first automatic framework' should be qualified given this narrow scope

Critical evidence accessibility concerns: Support F1 scores of only 0.17-0.22 (Table 3) indicate that retrieving complete evidence sets is very difficult. Large gap between Recall@20 (0.7) and Support F1 (0.2) suggests synthesized questions may be unrealistically hard for practical systems, undermining claims about 'authenticity'

Evaluation methodology limitations: Only 100 samples evaluated for main quality metrics (small sample size); LLM-as-judge approach, while theoretically justified, lacks direct validation against human judgment; no correlation analysis provided; limited systematic error analysis

Success rate and retry overhead: ~75% success rate (Table 4) requires ~25% of attempts to fail and retry. Average 1.17 attempts per success represents significant overhead not fully reflected in cost analysis. Inconsistent with 'fully automatic' claims

Unvalidated generalization: Tested only on English Wikipedia (Dec 2018 dump). No evidence approach transfers to other corpora (news, scientific papers, domain-specific texts). Fine-tuned reranker and MMR parameters may be Wikipedia-specific

Unexplained Q-Only vs Q+Docs performance gap: 25-point drop (comparison: 94%→69% EM) suggests questions may encode solvable signals. Insufficient analysis of whether questions genuinely require document integration vs. encoding weak signals
Fairness of human dataset comparison: Different annotation guidelines, Wikipedia versions, and creation processes make direct quality comparison potentially confounded
Dependency on proprietary models: Best results (Gemini 98.6%) use closed-source models; open-source alternatives degrade to 89.8%, raising reproducibility concerns despite stated commitment

Bridge entity identification not validated: No analysis of how often LLM-selected entities actually function as bridges; entity disambiguation/ambiguity issues not addressed; potential for spurious bridges

Modest improvements for strong models: Polisher module provides minimal gains for Gemini (95.2%→96.4%), questioning its complexity cost. Combined with low Support F1 scores, raises questions about fundamental synthesis quality

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a significant challenge in MHQA dataset creation
Sophisticated methodology with elegant components (fine-tuned reranker via simulated feedback, two-stage retrieval with clear constraints)
Comprehensive multi-dimensional evaluation system (LLM-as-judge, answerability/difficulty, evidence-accessibility, end-to-end RAG evaluation)
Extensive experimental validation across multiple LLM generators, large-scale stability testing (500 samples), and manual verification (92% reasoning path correctness)
Valuable finding that synthesized dataset exposes limitations in advanced RAG systems that don't generalize from established benchmarks
Strong reproducibility: public code, detailed prompts, cost analysis, comprehensive experimental settings
Formal problem definitions with constraints ensuring genuine multi-hop reasoning
weaknesses: Limited scope: only 2 of 5+ MHQA question types (bridge and comparison); leaves intersection, commonsense reasoning unaddressed

Evaluation methodology concerns: paper critiques human evaluation reliability (F.2) yet relies heavily on LLM judges; inter-human agreement (Fleiss' κ=0.46) only 'fair'; claims of 'surpassing' human datasets rest on LLM evaluation
Single-corpus evaluation: only English Wikipedia (Dec 2018); no cross-domain or cross-language evaluation limiting generalization claims
LLM dependency issues: quality bounded by generator LLM; closed-source models show output drift (reproducibility concern); unexplained gap in multi-hop rates across models (89.8% to 98.9%)

Methodological gaps: entity/attribute filtering thresholds adopted from single model (arbitrary); retrieval parameters determined via 'preliminary experiments' without ablation; no sensitivity analysis on key hyperparameters

Insufficient quality analysis: Polisher module performs REWORKED restructuring on questions (suggesting inconsistent base generation); 6% of reasoning paths have 'Information Gap Errors'; 59% of QA failures attributed to logical reasoning errors (unclear if model or question design)
Weak baseline comparison: Table 1 uses selective question type subsets (not random samples); no comparison with recent synthesis methods despite relevance
Limited human validation scale: only 50 pairwise comparisons and 100 reasoning paths despite focusing on evaluation methodology
Missing ablations: hyperparameter sensitivity, entity/attribute filtering threshold effects, Polisher module necessity beyond appendix ablation
Presentation issues: dense paper with critical details in 10+ appendices; Figure 2 complex and difficult to parse

strengths: Addresses genuine and timely problem: automated MHQA dataset creation at scale for specialized domains where human annotation is expensive

Exemplary three-dimensional evaluation framework combining LLM-as-judge (with principled self-consistency criterion), answerability/difficulty metrics, and evidence-accessibility analysis; goes well beyond typical dataset papers
Sophisticated methodology with well-motivated design choices: two-stage coarse-to-fine retrieval, simulation-based reranker fine-tuning, and systematic question polishing and validation
Strong empirical results: synthesized questions achieve 96.4-98.9% multi-hop rates and quality scores (4.27-4.45) comparable to or exceeding human benchmarks (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue)
Comprehensive experimental validation including 500-sample large-scale study, 92% human-LLM alignment, 92% correct reasoning paths, and thorough ablation studies demonstrating component contributions
Cost-effective (≈$7.90 per 1000 questions with Gemini) compared to expensive manual annotation; applicable to any raw corpus
Excellent reproducibility: complete prompts, detailed experimental settings, model specifications, and code release promised
End-to-end RAG evaluation reveals value: advanced retrieval methods sometimes underperform on synthesized data, suggesting dataset effectively exposes system limitations
weaknesses: Limited scope: addresses only 2 of ~5 MHQA question patterns (bridge, comparison); Table 5 shows human datasets include 15-21% intersection and other types, limiting claims of comprehensive synthesis
English/Wikipedia-only evaluation; no exploration of multilingual effectiveness or transfer to specialized domains despite strong motivation for domain applicability

LLM-as-judge evaluation concerns: while self-consistency argument is thoughtful, human validation study is small (50 pairwise comparisons, κ=0.46 inter-rater agreement); main results on 100 samples; judge selection and disagreement analysis not discussed

Quality ceiling tied to generator LLM capabilities: even best-performing Gemini shows 96.4% multi-hop rate; smaller models exhibit higher rejection rates (GLM-4-9B: 10.2%), suggesting limited scalability

Low evidence-accessibility metrics raise practical concerns: Support F1 consistently 0.17-0.22 (Table 3) means retrieving complete evidence sets is extremely difficult; tension with answerability claims not adequately addressed; Q+Docs performance gaps (Table 2) suggest questions may not be truly answerable from provided evidence

Missing experimental comparisons with synthesis baselines (Source2Synth, LLM+KG, MINTQA, etc.) despite literature review; claims these lack validation but direct comparison would strengthen positioning

Potential circularity in simulation-based reranker training: fine-tuning simulates the synthesis pipeline itself; modest ablation gains (coarse 70.9% → rerank 71.2% → fine-tune 75.3%) raise questions about necessity and overfitting
No systematic analysis of biases: paper acknowledges synthesis may inherit Wikipedia biases but provides no demographic or representation bias analysis despite recognizing this as a limitation

Incomplete error analysis: only GPT-4o failures examined; 6% 'Information Gap' errors suggest evidence insufficiency; no analysis of smaller model failure modes or true answerability given stated evidence
Claim of 'authenticity' is somewhat circular: authenticity demonstrated through LLM evaluation itself; human alignment study small (50 pairs) and may not be representative
